title: Pilot study of provider adherence to language services for surgical patients with limited English proficiency
author: J Walker Rosenthal

evds.title: Documented interpreter use was not significantly associated with LOS, ED revisits, readmission, or surgical follow-up after cholecystectomy
evds.finding: In LEP cholecystectomy patients, documented interpreter use was not significantly associated with any of the four 30-day postoperative outcomes examined: length of stay (LOS 59.17 vs 44.9 hours, p=0.4114), ED revisits (9.1% vs 6.9%, p=0.558), readmission (4.2% vs 4.6%, p=0.885), or surgical follow-up (51.0% vs 51.7%, p=0.921) (Table 5). These are null/non-significant associations in a study the authors describe as likely underpowered for these infrequent clinical outcomes.

evds.title: Interpreter use was documented for only 62% of LEP cholecystectomy patients despite the Section 1557 mandate
evds.finding: Among LEP patients undergoing cholecystectomy at a single academic health system, documented interpreter use during the preoperative informed-consent process was present for only 62% of patients (141 of 228), well below the full compliance required by Section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act. Of those with documented use, most was by a professional interpreter (n=126, 55%) while 7% used an ad-hoc interpreter (Table 3).

evds.title: Language-concordant documentation was not significantly associated with LOS, ED revisits, readmission, or surgical follow-up after cholecystectomy
evds.finding: In LEP cholecystectomy patients, receipt of language-concordant paperwork was not significantly associated with any 30-day postoperative outcome: length of stay (LOS 60.45 vs 50.90 hours, p=0.604), ED revisits (4.3% vs 9.9%, p=0.158), readmission (4.3% vs 4.3%, p=1.000), or surgical follow-up (55.1% vs 49.7%, p=0.454), comparing 69 patients with concordant vs 161 with discordant paperwork (Table 5). These are null/non-significant associations in a study the authors describe as likely underpowered for these infrequent clinical outcomes.

evds.title: Only 31% of LEP cholecystectomy patients received language-concordant documentation
evds.finding: Among LEP patients undergoing cholecystectomy, only 31% (69 of 228) received any language-concordant paperwork (translated consent form and/or discharge documents). Fully language-concordant consent forms were present for only 21% (n=47), and complete language-concordant discharge documents for only 13% (n=28); most patients (75%, n=168) had only partially concordant discharge documents (Supplementary Table 1).

candidates: Interpreter use was documented for 62.2% of LEP patients undergoing cholecystectomy.
Only 30% of LEP patients received language concordant documentation.
Interpreter service utilization was not significantly associated with length of stay.
Interpreter service utilization was not significantly associated with emergency department re-visits.
Interpreter service utilization was not significantly associated with hospital readmissions.
Interpreter service utilization was not significantly associated with surgeon follow-up.

abstractAnchors.text: Interpreter use was documented for 62.2 ​% of patients and 30 ​% received language concordant documentation.
Interpreter service utilization and language concordant documentation were not significantly associated with LOS, ED visits, hospital readmissions, or surgeon follow-up.
Language interpreter services are underutilized for LEP patients.
These findings suggest the need for further investigation into the barriers to providing this service for patients during a time of critical decision-making.
